speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: asked the Minister for Health to what extent should informed consent for minor medical procedures be sought from patients that will be considered reasonably detailed and effective and not lead to the practice of defensive medicine and drive up costs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I understand Mr Murali Pillai1 had also filed a similar question on this issue and I hope that my reply will address the queries raised by the Member.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: First, let me briefly set out the background.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Lim Lian Arn is an orthopaedic surgeon.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: His patient complained that Dr Lim had failed to advise her on the possible complications arising from an injection of a steroid and local anesthetic injection, also commonly known as H&L Injection.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Lim's treatment of the patient was found to be appropriate.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But he did not advise nor document in the patient’s medical records the possible complications or the patient’s consent.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Through his lawyers, Dr Lim asked for the maximum fine of $100,000 in lieu of suspension or, if the DT decided that suspension was warranted, a three-month suspension.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Singapore Medical Council (SMC) had sought a suspension of five months.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Both Dr Lim and SMC did not appeal the sentence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Members have asked how this case would affect the future practice of medicine, with regard to informed consent and what constitutes material information.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Members also asked if the penalty was commensurate with similar cases in the past, and how the Ministry of Health (MOH) would assure doctors that only egregious cases will attract heavy penalties.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Overall, Members were concerned about whether the decision will lead to defensive practices and increasing healthcare costs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: From 2013 to 2018, SMC convened Complaints Committees (CCs) to investigate over 900 complaints.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And in about 92% of these cases, the CCs were of the view that no formal inquiry by a DT was necessary.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In those cases referred to DT, the profession accepted the DTs’ findings and sentences in most of them.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Only in a few cases were questions raised.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is wrong to infer that the decision makes it mandatory for a doctor to lay out and get the consent of a patient for every possible side effect and potential complications of a drug or treatment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Lim admitted that he was guilty of failing to inform the patient of any risks and complications; he was not found guilty for failing to inform the patient of all possible complications that could arise from the H&L Injection.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Under the SMC Ethical Code and Ethical Guidelines (ECEG), doctors are to disclose relevant and material information to their patients, while remote risks with minor consequences will generally be deemed immaterial and need not be disclosed.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: What a doctor needs to inform a patient about prior to a treatment or procedure continues to depend on the specific facts of the case, including the particular circumstances of the patient.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, what is considered material information was not the issue before the DT in Dr Lim's case, and the DT did not apply the modified Montgomery Test as Dr Lim conceded that he had not informed the patient of any risks or complications at all.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ultimately, the DT decided that the maximum fine of $100,000 requested by Dr Lim's lawyer would be the appropriate sentence.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There can be questions as to whether this was too high a fine and why the SMC was asking for a five-month suspension.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There has been considerable concern in the medical profession about the maximum fine having been imposed and that, at one point, suspension was considered.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The concerns are understandable when considering the facts and circumstances of this case.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Many fair-minded doctors would think that the penalty imposed was harsh.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The appointment of a Sentencing Guidelines Committee on 1 January 2019 will, therefore, help in ensuring consistency and fairness in the sentences meted, and improve transparency and rigour in the disciplinary process.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There has been feedback on the considerable confusion amongst medical practitioners on the requirements on informed consent and material information, and how the modified Montgomery Test and the ECEG should apply.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We want to take steps to reassure the profession – and to clarify the position – as MOH does not want the profession to go down the path of defensive medicine.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We acknowledge that the profession needs assurance on what the legal position is, and what the procedures/punishments are when disciplinary proceedings are undertaken.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will need to discuss the issues with the profession, in the context of a broader review of the current rules, processes and legal position, to achieve the above outcome.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While SMC administers the disciplinary process, the CCs and DTs, comprised substantially of senior doctors, make decisions independently of SMC.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In arriving at their decisions, the CCs and DTs also obtain the opinions of experts who are peers of the respondent doctor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The DT says that the doctors do not have to disclose all side effects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we have seen that, in this case, for the H&L injection, it was listed out from (a) to (g) the side effects that Dr Lim should have informed and noted in the case notes for the patient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it seems as though that although the DT says that the doctor does not have to list all the side effects to the patient, yet, at the same time, the charge is precisely that he had failed to list out all the side effects and that he should have done so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I could read out (a) to (g) but it would be very long, and that is precisely the point.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because it is a very long list, and the consultation would drag on for very long for the doctor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the question is: for MOH, when it says material information is all that is needed, how?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it (a) to (f), (a) to (e) or (c) to (f)?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many side effects would be material information?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if the doctor informs the patient from (a) to (e) and leaves out (f), and if the patient gets (f) as a side effect, would then the doctor be liable?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: What is important is that the doctor needs to inform patients complications or side effects that are relevant to the patient.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the grounds of the decision by the DT in this case, I note that there were six possible complications that were listed from (a) to (f).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But I would like to reassure Members of the House as well as the medical profession that these are just examples of some of the possible complications that Dr Lim could have told the patient.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, in this case, it is not a matter of whether sufficient complications or side effects had been counselled; rather, it is the case whereby Dr Lim had failed to even inform the patient of any possible side effects.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The medical fraternity currently has rallied, including with the public coming in, to raise a petition against this whole issue.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Even for the public, they felt that this $100,000 fine is a little too excessive.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Yes, I agree with the Senior Minister of State that it is self-regulatory, but self-regulatory does not mean no regulation at all.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: MOH should still have an oversight over SMC.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: My question then is: what is MOH's position and will this $100,000 fine be reviewed again rather than to leave it as it is?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If we leave it as it is, then the medical fraternity will just say that there is no change in everything else, which means that we still could be fined $100,000.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If we miss out just one side effect, we could be fined.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Particular to this case, we note that Dr Lim's lawyer had actually requested either $100,000 fine in lieu of suspension, or, if the DT decided on suspension, a period of three months.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Of course, this is based on past precedents, as noted by both SMC and the defendant's counsel.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My question revolves around the fact that in the recent past, I see that doctors were somehow disquieted by SMC's rulings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the medical profession is meant to be self-regulating, as mentioned by the hon Senior Minister of State, how do we address the gap between what is understood by the medical profession on one hand and the SMC's rulings meted out by senior doctors?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In that regard, I note that there are sentencing guidelines that would be issued.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What other steps can be taken to address this gap?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While SMC administers the disciplinary process, the CCs and DTs, comprised substantially of senior doctors, make the decision independently of SMC.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: So far, based on the statistics that I have given in my reply, the majority of DT findings and sentences were accepted by the medical profession.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Only a small number of cases attracted some questions with regard to the decisions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But based on these statistics, we can see that, actually, the self-regulatory processes are working very well.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I do understand there are some concerns with regard to informed consent as well as material information, and we will engage the medical community to clarify some of these doubts that they may have.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I would just like to ask the Senior Minister of State again: in the past, there have been precedents whereby DTs have thrown out certain cases but, in the end, upon appealing to the Ministers, the DT has to reopen the case again.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In this case now, it is the direct opposite, which means that the DT has already decided, whether, currently, since there is a petition from both the public as well as from the medical fraternity to the Ministry, will the Minister now consider reopening this case?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But having said that, we will continue to look at some of the concerns of the medical profession.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In fact, we will be engaging the three professional bodies of the medical profession to see how we can address some of these concerns.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: At the same time, if necessary, we will review the disciplinary processes in the form of amending the Medical Registration Act.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And, if necessary, even amending other laws, moving forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Ministry then consider having it into the Statutes, so that it makes things a lot clearer?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And what is the Senior Minister of State's view on the implications on clinical practice till the day we get clarity on this test?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To put things in perspective, the Modified Montgomery Test was introduced in the Court of Appeal decision recently and not by MOH or SMC.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Prior to the Court of Appeal's decision in Hii Chii Kok's case in 2017, it was settled law in Singapore that the assessment of whether a doctor has met the requisite standard of care in all aspects of his interaction with the patient should be made with reference to the practices and opinions of a responsible body of medical practitioners although such practices and opinions must be logically defensible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This test, like what Mr Desmond Choo has mentioned, is also known as the Bolam-Bolitho test.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I am clearly aware of the concerns of many medical professionals on the Modified Montgomery Test.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I have personally received feedback from fellow medical practitioners, especially on the requirement on informed consent and material information, and how this new test should be applied.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There is also feedback from the medical community that this may lead to defensive medicine and escalation of healthcare costs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH is aware and understands the apprehension and the confusion and uncertainty on the ground.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State, with the changeover to the Modified Montgomery Test and also taking the Hii Chii Kok case as an example – which, of course, has its pros and cons as well – moving forward, because we practise in a restructured hospital where there are lots and lots of junior doctors and personnel in training who are performing procedures almost every day and taking consent, so, perhaps, will MOH be able to come up with some kind of standardised guidelines for doctors in practice as well as for specialists?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And also, perhaps to do some focus group discussions not only with the senior representatives but also with the junior level doctors, because they are the ones for whom we need to allay their anxieties, and they are the ones running the clinics, whether through direct supervision or indirect supervision by seniors and consultants; they are the ones who are running our clinics and the hospitals in the restructured hospital setting these days.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Indeed, we need to continue to provide education to the medical profession with regard to proper documentation as well as consent-taking.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In fact, it is important that the medical professionals properly document the management of patients under their care because properly kept medical records form the basis of good management of the patient and sound communications pertaining to the care of the patient.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Anecdotally, it seems that many complaints by patients could have been avoided if their doctors had communicated with them better.
